impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. The case involves blockbuster migraine drugs (Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's competing product) and has major implications for how courts evaluate written description and enablement for antibody claims defined by function.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug innovators by affirming that genus claims to humanized antibodies defined by function can satisfy § 112 requirements, supporting the enforceability of valuable pharmaceutical patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates potential barriers for generic and biosimilar competitors seeking to enter the anti-CGRP migraine treatment market, and may increase patent litigation risk for companies developing competing biologics in the same therapeutic space.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional patent constituted an obvious typographical error correctable without adding new matter, thereby entitling the patent to the provisional's earlier priority date and avoiding anticipation by Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the alteration from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error and introduced new matter not supported by the provisional application. Because the patent lost its earlier priority date, Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims, invalidating the patent covering compounds related to Paxlovid.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects companies like Pfizer from patent claims that attempt to retroactively capture priority over publicly disclosed compounds through post-hoc corrections to provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Warns pharmaceutical patentees that even minor drafting errors in provisional applications can be fatal to patent validity if they affect claim scope, emphasizing the critical importance of precise provisional application drafting.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in its handling of damages for trade secret misappropriation under the DTSA and MUTSA, and whether the jury's breach of contract damages award should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The decision affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Expands the range of permissible damages models in trade secret misappropriation cases, giving plaintiffs greater flexibility to present unjust enrichment and other theories; also reinforces jury authority on contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license or access third-party software face heightened misappropriation liability risk, particularly when developing replacement products during or after a licensing relationship.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim under the Defend Trade Secrets Act was time-barred where Insulet had knowledge of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and judgment for Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. Despite evidence that EOFlow hired former Insulet employees who shared proprietary CAD files, design information, and algorithms for insulin patch pump development, the court determined Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation too early for its 2023 complaint to be timely.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on DTSA statute of limitations accrual, giving defendants a strong defense when plaintiffs delay filing suit despite knowledge of potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they do not act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation, even while continuing to investigate the scope of harm.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets related to a cosmetic penile implant were protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether the inventorship determination on related patents should be reversed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, holding that plaintiffs failed to prove each asserted trade secret was protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction. It also reversed the patent invalidity finding based on inventorship, since the contribution found by the jury was now determined to involve generally known ideas. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces the requirement that trade secret claimants must prove that each asserted secret is not generally known, providing defendants with a stronger basis to challenge vague or overbroad trade secret assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs face a higher evidentiary bar to establish protectability, particularly where the claimed secrets overlap with publicly available knowledge in the field.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not raised in its IPR petition but that a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve on two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and failure to account for hindsight bias on the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous proof that prior art references were reasonably discoverable by a skilled searcher at the time of the original IPR petition.
impacts.positiveImplications: Benefits accused infringers by limiting the circumstances under which IPR estoppel bars them from raising invalidity defenses in district court, preserving more robust opportunities to challenge patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased difficulty in using IPR estoppel to streamline district court litigation, as defendants retain broader ability to raise new invalidity grounds not presented in earlier IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part and affirmed in part the grant of summary judgment to Intel, addressing the territorial scope of patent infringement for semiconductor technology and the viability of doctrine of equivalents arguments. The court also addressed the district court's striking of damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies boundaries of patent infringement liability for multinational technology companies regarding extraterritorial activities, potentially limiting exposure for overseas manufacturing and testing.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent holders may face greater difficulty establishing infringement when accused activities have significant extraterritorial components.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patentee who licenses certain rights exclusively but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement possesses a non-illusory exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III standing. The decision clarifies the standing analysis for patent owners who have entered complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides patent owners greater certainty that they can retain and exercise the right to sue for infringement even after granting exclusive licenses, facilitating flexible licensing structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from both patent owners and exclusive licensees under complex licensing arrangements, complicating settlement and defense strategies.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that asked a single question on infringement covering all asserted patents, without identifying which patent(s) were infringed, required vacatur of the infringement and damages judgments, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 eligibility analysis under Alice step two.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, holding that the single-question verdict form on infringement across all four asserted patents was flawed. The court also vacated and remanded the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent for further proceedings under Alice step two, while affirming eligibility for two other patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces procedural protections for accused infringers by requiring patent-specific verdict questions, preventing ambiguous general verdicts that may conflate distinct patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs must ensure verdict forms clearly delineate infringement findings for each asserted patent, or risk vacatur of significant damages awards.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, creating a split outcome on § 101 for closely related patents in the communications technology space. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, sustaining a willful infringement finding against LG Electronics for its television products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that certain applied technology improvements to digital communication standards can satisfy § 101, supporting patent enforcement against standard-essential technology implementers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards face continued risk of patent infringement liability and damages, even for standards-based implementations.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285. The decision continues the trend of invalidating agricultural technology patents as abstract under Alice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech companies accused of infringement benefit from the continued application of § 101 to invalidate broadly claimed data-collection patents, reducing litigation exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology innovators face difficulty patenting data collection and processing systems, and the vacatur on the exceptional case finding signals potential fee-shifting risk for patent plaintiffs asserting ineligible claims.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose a device's internal functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and rejecting the argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of a device's functionality. The ruling confirms that commercial sales of a device embodying claimed features trigger § 102(b) regardless of whether the buyer knew the device's internal workings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens invalidity defenses by confirming that prior commercial sales of products embodying claimed features trigger the on-sale bar even without public disclosure of internal functionality, and that 30(b)(6) testimony is broadly admissible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges based on historical product sales, even when the prior art product's internal mechanisms were not publicly known.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after missing the statutory deadline for seeking a stay of the original action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for mandatory stays by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The decision prevents strategic manipulation of the § 1659(a) mandatory stay provision and preserves the ability of patent holders to pursue parallel ITC and district court proceedings without indefinite delay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects patent holders and ITC complainants from strategic delay tactics by respondents who might otherwise refile district court actions to obtain mandatory stays they failed to timely request.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay cannot cure the deficiency through refiling, limiting their ability to coordinate ITC and district court proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination of a sensor-based logistics tracking patent, and whether a non-party to the underlying district court litigation may file an IPR petition at the one-year statutory deadline of a party to that litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding on challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raises significant questions about potential abuse of the IPR system by entities filing petitions on behalf of or in coordination with time-barred litigants. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit from closer scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by non-parties suspected of acting as proxies for time-barred parties, potentially curbing strategic IPR abuse.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur creates uncertainty for companies relying on IPR outcomes to clear patent obstacles, particularly in the logistics and IoT technology sectors.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims surviving an IPR can be dismissed on the pleadings as obvious on the same grounds that invalidated other claims of the same patent, and whether the district court properly awarded attorney fees under § 285 and sanctions under § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage but reversed the exceptional case finding under § 285 and attorney sanctions under § 1927, holding that the grounds presented were insufficient to support either award. The decision establishes that surviving IPR does not immunize claims from invalidity challenges on the same grounds, while raising the bar for fee-shifting and sanctions against patent plaintiffs.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides patent defendants an efficient mechanism to dismiss infringement claims at the pleading stage based on IPR-established prior art, while the reversal of fees and sanctions protects patent plaintiffs from excessive penalties for asserting surviving claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders whose patents partially survive IPR face risk that remaining claims can still be dismissed as obvious on the same grounds, undermining the value of partial IPR victories.
